subject: Livestream gateway: intermittent header fragmentation causing stream errors
messages:
From: Michael Torres <michael.torres@brightwave.com>
To: alex_martinez@redwood.com
Cc: Sarah Lin <sarah.lin@brightwave.com>
Date: Mon, 09 Jul 2028 08:42:00 -0700
Subject: Live streaming spikes / 502s and timeouts impacting on-air widgets

Alex —

We're seeing repeated 502s and stalled frames from the Redwood live endpoint used by our on-air widgets starting ~07:30 PST. Latency for stream open has jumped from ~120ms to 800ms on average, and error-rate for token renewals is up ~9%. This is customer-visible (three broadcasters reported freezes during live segments).

Attached is our server-side error log and a pcap capture from the gateway. We traced the library calls and saw the client re-open stream attempts with truncated header blocks immediately before the failures. Not sure if this is a Redwood-side regression or the recently-updated client SDK.

Can we get an urgent triage and a hotfix timeline? We have execs on standby.

—Michael
Director, Platform Engineering
BrightWave Labs

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Live streaming spikes / 502s and timeouts impacting on-air widgets

Thanks for the data, Michael. I've had a look at the pcap and the server logs. Initial read: we're seeing header blocks split across multiple HTTP/2 frames in a pattern that our streaming parser's incremental header reassembly doesn't expect after certain fragmentation sizes. The parser then discards the header-set and treats the stream as malformed, which yields a 502 back to the client and triggers the SDK reconnect logic — explains the elevated error-rate and latency.

This is consistent with an edge case introduced when we optimized flushing for larger KV cache writes in the runtime last month; the runtime can emit smaller header frames in quick succession which exercises the client-side header reassembly path. Affected flows correlate with long initial prompt sizes and some vendor proxies that re-chunk frames (the pcap shows re-chunking for a subset of requests).

Planned actions (immediate):
- Karthik and I will instrument a hotfix branch that makes header reassembly tolerant to split header fragments and add explicit backpressure when the KV cache flush is active.
- Temporary mitigation: we can provide a small SDK patch that forces the client to buffer header fragments until the header-complete flag is observed. That is low-risk and should be deliverable in ~2–3 hours for a patch release.
- Ops mitigation: we will put a traffic rule at the gateway to coalesce frames for affected customers to reduce re-chunking while the patch is prepared.

Request from Michael: if you can share any specific request IDs for the events in your logs we can pin them to our traces — helpful for verification.

Marissa
Staff Software Engineer, Runtime
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Live streaming spikes / 502s and timeouts impacting on-air widgets

Update for execs and BrightWave:

1) Impact assessment: engineering has mapped the BrightWave request IDs to internal traces — confirmed clients saw ~7–11% elevated 502/stream-reset error-rate for the 07:30–08:00 PST window. We've classified this as a P0 customer impact event for BrightWave (severity qualifies under our SLA definitions).

2) Fix & timeline: Marissa and Karthik delivered an SDK patch (sdk_workaround_v0.1.diff) that instructs the client to buffer header fragments and to retry handshakes more gracefully. We've deployed a gateway frame-coalescing rule that mitigates re-chunking for BrightWave traffic and rolled the SDK patch to their staging fleet. Initial verification shows error-rate dropped to baseline within 45 minutes of the mitigation.

3) Next steps:
- Today: Roll the SDK patch to BrightWave production (scheduled 12:30 PST) — patch is low-risk, non-breaking.
- 48h: Backport the parser tolerance changes into runtime and the official SDK (v1.8.3) with tests and broader canary.
- 1 week: Postmortem with BrightWave and exec summary; action items to detect fragment-induced parser failures automatically.

We're prepared to discuss SLA crediting once the postmortem quantifies customer-visible duration; Rafael will coordinate on contract implications.

Alex Martinez
